item.title: Next week in Miami: AI, cyber risk and the next cycle
item.description: 57% of North American family offices reported a cyberattack. The question we bring to our 1 December dinner, and last seats for both events.

item.content:encoded:
Operating Advantage, Friday Note: AI raises the stakes. So does cyber risk.

A short Friday note before our two Miami events next week. To our US readers, we hope the Thanksgiving weekend is a good one.

The question

Is cyber risk now an investment risk?

Capital is moving into AI faster than ever. AI accounted for a record 82.7% of US venture deal value in 2026 through the third quarter, which reached $515.8 billion (PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor via SiliconANGLE, October 2026).

The attack surface is moving with it. In Deloitte's 2024 Family Office Cybersecurity Report, 43% of family offices globally had suffered a cyberattack in the prior 12 to 24 months, rising to 57% in North America, and 31% had no incident response plan (WealthBriefing, April 2025). In a 2025 Omega Systems survey, 83% of family offices said they worry about deepfake and impersonation attacks on their principals (Family Wealth Report, April 2026).

AI and cyber risk in three numbers.


Our view: AI makes a portfolio company more valuable and more exposed at the same time. Cyber readiness belongs in due diligence next to revenue quality, not in a checklist after closing.

Three questions we will bring to the table on 1 December:

  1. How should an investor price cyber risk into an AI-heavy portfolio?

  2. What changes in the next investment cycle after the midterms?

  3. Which controls should a family office expect from the managers and companies it backs?

From the studio

MortgageFlow

The same principle applies inside our own studio. MortgageFlow, built in our xPL Ventures studio, works with sensitive borrower files, so security is part of the product from the first version, not an add-on. The product vision video is here: MortgageFlow product vision.

item.title: Six million owners are retiring. Who buys the companies?
item.description: A preview of our 3 December breakfast in Miami, and last call for both events.
item.dc:creator: EPL Group
item.content:encoded:
Operating Advantage, Issue 2: Six million owners are retiring. Who buys the companies?

The question

Six million owners are retiring. Who buys the companies?

More than half of US small-business owners are now over 55, up from roughly 30% in 2002. About 6 million small and mid-sized businesses will face an ownership change by 2035, and more than 1 million of them are viable for sale, representing up to $5 trillion in enterprise value (McKinsey, February 2026).

Today most of that value disappears. Of about 510,000 small-business exits in 2022, 92% were closures, 5% were sales and 3% were transfers to new owners, often within the family (McKinsey, same report).

The great ownership transfer in three numbers.

Our view: for the owner of a cash-generating company, the buyer matters as much as the price. The acquirers who win in the lower middle market bring a clear operating plan for the day after closing, and enough patience to carry it out.

This is the question on the table at our breakfast debate on 3 December: where value is really created in Sunbelt acquisitions, from sourcing and structuring to the operating plan after closing.

The explainer

Permanent capital vs a buyout fund

A traditional buyout fund buys a company, improves it and sells it, usually within three to seven years, because the fund has to return capital to its investors in about 10 years. Returns come mostly at exit.

A permanent capital vehicle has no fixed end date. It can be an evergreen fund, a holding company or a long-life fund. Returns come mostly from the cash the companies generate each year, with exits only when they make sense. Permanent Equity, one of the best-known examples, invests out of 30-year funds (Permanent Equity).

Buyout fund vs permanent capital, side by side.

What investors gain: lower transaction costs, compounding without forced sales, and a better offer to founders who want continuity. What they give up: fewer liquidity events, so they need a clear policy on distributions and exits.

From the studio

MortgageFlow

Acquisitions and mortgages share a problem: deals slow down when the file is incomplete. MortgageFlow, built in our xPL Ventures studio, checks a mortgage file against lender requirements before it is submitted. If you missed it last week, the product vision video is here: MortgageFlow product vision.

The broker channel is growing. So is the paperwork.

Welcome to Operating Advantage, a weekly note from the partners at EPL Group. Each issue takes one question about where capital meets operating know-how, answers it with data, and shares what we are building and where to meet us. No pitches, no fund offerings.

The question

Why does a growing broker channel still check files by hand?

Canadians are moving to mortgage brokers. In Mortgage Professionals Canada's February 2026 survey, 38% of recent buyers used a broker, up six points, and 48% of first-time buyers did (CMP, July 2026).

Each file is also harder to place. Nearly 80% of brokers sent deals to five or more lenders in 2025, up from 73%, and brokers named documentation overload among their main challenges (CMP Brokers on Lenders, September 2025). Every lender brings its own rules and its own document list.

And volume stays high. CMHC expects about 1.15 million mortgages to renew in 2026 and another 940,000 in 2027 (CMP, December 2025).

Our view: more files, more lenders and more rules land on the same number of broker hours. The fastest gain is catching what is missing before the file leaves the broker, not after the lender sends it back.

From the studio

MortgageFlow

MortgageFlow, built in our xPL Ventures studio, is an AI pre-underwriting tool for Canadian mortgage brokers. It reviews a borrower's file against what lenders require before submission, so the broker finds the gaps first, not the lender.
